reconcile.connective: Commentators read "swear not at all" as aimed at the rabbis' evasive, frivolous oaths, not at the solemn oath by God's name the Torah commands.

discrepancy.connective: The Skeptic's Annotated Bible presses the pair head-on, setting the Torah's command to "swear by his name" against Jesus' flat "swear not at all" and James' "above all things... swear not."

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.work: The Skeptic's Annotated Bible, "Is it OK to take oaths?" (skepticsannotatedbible.com/contra/oaths.html)
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, The Skeptic's Annotated Bible (2013), "Is it OK to take oaths?"

excerpts.excerpt_text: But I say unto you, Swear not at all—That this was meant to condemn swearing of every kind and on every occasion—as the Society of Friends and some other ultra-moralists allege—is not for a moment to be thought. For even Jehovah is said once and again to have sworn by Himself … Evidently, it is swearing in common intercourse and on frivolous occasions that is here meant.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly denies that 'swear not at all' forbids all oaths (the heart of the contradiction), grounding the harmonization in God's own swearing and limiting the target to frivolous/common-intercourse oaths — the strongest single reconcile voice on the row; parity-capped to one against the named-skeptic discrepancy pole.

pd_work.resource: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible (1706-14), on Matthew 5:33-37
pd_work.author: Matthew Henry
pd_work.note: Henry harmonizes this exact pair: 'Not that all swearing is sinful; so far from that, if rightly done, it is a part of religious worship,' citing Deut 6:13; 10:20; Jer 4:2 — the OT swearing commands at issue. Used in place of Haley, whose specific coverage of this pair could not be confirmed.
